Any form of physical contact with others
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.explanation: The profile is for a 61-year-old bus driver who witnessed trauma. 'Bicycle' as a trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it points toward a very specific accident scenario that is not supported elsewhere in the report. The other items emphasize guilt, sensory reliving, and contamination/interpersonal avoidance, creating a mixed picture that is hard to unify around a single witnessed-trauma account.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is much more characteristic of sexual or contact-based interpersonal trauma than of witnessed trauma. For a witnessed-trauma formulation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile unless there was direct bodily involvement, which is not reflected elsewhere.

Avoiding sex is hard to explain from the rest of this profile. The selected memory and appraisal items center on reliving and guilt about inaction, but do not support a coherent mechanism for sexual avoidance in a witnessed-trauma case.

vignette: Lucia sat behind the wheel of her city bus, the familiar hum of the engine steady beneath her feet, when the silver sedan swerved into her lane. It was not her fault, but the way the metal buckled, the sudden spray of crimson across the asphalt, and the sharp cry of an elderly passenger as she fell against the glass made Lucia freeze. She had come to believe that the moment the tires screeched, she had already failed to protect the people riding with her. What frightened her most was the blood, not just on the road, but in her mind’s eye, staining her own sleeves and the faces of those she carried. The weeks that followed were quiet, but the memory did not settle into the past. When it returned, it arrived fully formed, a complete sensory flood: the smell of hot brakes, the vibration of the crash against her palms, the sound of glass cracking, all at once. Sometimes, without any clear picture, a wave of raw fear would catch her in the kitchen, making her grip the counter until her knuckles whitened. She felt the event unfolding right now, not something tucked away in years. On the streets, Lucia’s route became a landscape of reminders. She stopped passengers from leaning against the handrails near her, flinching when a hand brushed her shoulder, certain that any physical contact might pull her back into that moment. She began performing quiet mental rituals, tracing invisible lines in the air or repeating a silent count of stops, holding the belief that the numbers kept the bad things at bay. When a couple laughed loudly nearby or when a wedding invitation landed in her mail, she would slip the cards into the top drawer, unable to bear the quiet weight of grief that gathered around lost birthdays and familiar faces. The bus depot, her daily anchor, offered little relief. Watching other drivers take their seats or sharing a quiet café con leche with her husband, Carlos, she wondered if her life was worth living when every glance at the road felt like a test she had already failed. She had never forgiven herself for not doing more, not holding the door tighter, not reaching out sooner, and that belief settled into her bones. Now, at sixty-one, Lucia drives the same route, but the streets feel closer, the cars more unpredictable. She still feels the sudden lurch of loss of control when a delivery van cuts too sharply, and the crash imagery of cars hit by accident lingers behind her eyes. Her mental rituals continue, her hands hover just above her thighs, and she avoids the heavy hugs her friends offer, preferring the company of empty seats. She has come to expect the emotion without the image, the sudden certainty that something is wrong before it even happens. What finally brought her to the clinic was not a single breakdown, but the quiet accumulation of a life measured in avoided touches and counted stops. She sits in the waiting room now, watching a taxi back up, feeling the familiar pressure in her chest as if the past were still pressing forward. She hopes someone can help her understand why the world feels so heavy, why she must keep the rituals and the distance, and why, despite the years, she still feels she did not do enough. She fears another crash, but she also hopes that someone might finally see that she is still here, still holding the line.
